Lecture 9 · Part 1The Salivary Glands

Lecturer: Dr Nur Hassan, BDS, PGT (Oral Surg), PhD — Senior Lecturer, CSU.

Major salivary glands

  • Parotid glands
  • Submandibular glands
  • Sublingual glands

Minor salivary glands

  • Throughout the oral cavity
  • 500–1000 of them, each 1–5 mm
GlandSize rankSecretionShape
ParotidLargestPurely serous — wateryPyramidal, up to 5 processes
SubmandibularSecond largestMixed, predominantly serousHook shaped
SublingualSmallestMixed, predominantly mucousAlmond shaped

Lecture 9 · Part 2Parotid Gland

  • Secretion: purely serous (watery)
  • Shape: pyramidal, with up to 5 processes
  • Capsule: the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
  • Location: lies over masseter (75%) and the retromandibular region (25%)

Borders

DirectionBoundary
PosteriorSternocleidomastoid
AnteriorRamus of the mandible and masseter
SuperiorExternal acoustic meatus and the zygomatic arch
InferiorPosterior belly of digastric

Lobes & duct

  • Lobes: superficial and deep, divided by the facial nerve
  • Duct: Stensen’s duct — forms within the deep lobe, passes anteriorly across masseter, then turns medially to penetrate buccinator and open into the oral cavity
  • Opening: at the parotid papilla, opposite the maxillary 2nd molar
Surgically critical: the facial nerve runs through the parotid, dividing it into superficial and deep lobes. Parotid surgery therefore always carries a risk of facial nerve injury, and the nerve must be identified and preserved.

Relations

  • The external carotid artery terminates within the gland into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries
  • The retromandibular vein lies within it
  • The facial nerve lies most laterally, branching into its five terminal branches
  • The deep lobe lies close to the carotid sheath and superior constrictor
  • The parotid capsule is innervated by the great auricular nerve
  • Bony relations: mastoid, styloid, zygomatic arch, external acoustic meatus, ramus of the mandible and SCM
Layer order, superficial → deep: facial nerve, then retromandibular vein, then external carotid artery. A useful way to remember it when identifying structures during dissection.

Lecture 9 · Part 3Submandibular & Sublingual Glands

Submandibular gland

  • Superficial part (larger) — in the submandibular fossa, inferior to the mylohyoid line
  • Deep part (smaller) — wraps around the posterior margin of mylohyoid, lying lateral to hyoglossus
  • Duct: Wharton’s duct, emerging from the medial side of the deep part
  • Opening: at the sublingual caruncles, beside the base of the lingual frenulum
Why submandibular stones are common: Wharton’s duct runs uphill from the gland to its opening, and the secretion is more viscous than the parotid’s — so this is the gland where sialoliths most often form.

Sublingual gland

  • Location: anterior floor of the oral cavity, between the oral mucosa and mylohyoid, in the sublingual fossa
  • Duct: multiple small excretory ducts — the minor sublingual ducts (Bartholin's ducts)
  • Opening: along the sublingual fold, or into the submandibular gland

Minor salivary glands

  • 700–1000 glands, predominantly mucous — except von Ebner’s glands, which are lingual serous glands in the circumvallate papillae
  • Produce only 5–8% of total salivary output, but keep the mouth moist when the major glands are not functioning
  • Distributed throughout the oral mucosa of the oral cavity and oropharynx — except the gingiva and the anterior part of the hard palate
  • Open directly onto the mucosa

Lecture 9 · Part 4Vascular Supply & Innervation

ParotidSubmandibular & sublingual
ArterialGlandular branches of the external carotid artery and the superficial temporal arteryFacial and lingual arteries
VenousExternal jugular veinFacial and lingual veins
LymphaticParotid nodes → superficial and deep cervical nodesSubmandibular nodes → deep cervical nodes (jugulo-omohyoid)

Parasympathetic innervation

GlandNerveGanglion
ParotidGlossopharyngeal (CN IX)Otic ganglion
All glands above the oral fissureGreater petrosal nerve (CN VII)Pterygopalatine ganglion
All glands below the oral fissure — including submandibular and sublingualChorda tympani (CN VII)Submandibular ganglion

Sympathetic supply to the submandibular and sublingual glands comes from the external carotid plexus.

The one that trips people up: the parotid is the odd gland out — it is the only major salivary gland supplied by CN IX rather than CN VII. The full pathway is IX → tympanic nerve → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve → parotid.

Lecture 9 · Part 5Infratemporal Fossa

DirectionBoundary
LateralRamus of the mandible
MedialLateral pterygoid plate
AnteriorMaxilla
PosteriorStyloid process and the mandibular condyle

Contents

Muscles of mastication

  • Medial pterygoid
  • Lateral pterygoid
  • Temporalis

Nerves

  • Branches of V3 — inferior alveolar, buccal, lingual, auriculotemporal
  • Chorda tympani (CN VII)
  • Otic ganglion — just below foramen ovale; supplies the parotid gland
Also in the fossa (from the blood supply lecture): the first two parts of the maxillary artery and the pterygoid venous plexus. Together with the nerves above, that makes this the space an inferior alveolar nerve block passes into.

Lecture 9 · Part 6Pterygopalatine Fossa

The pterygopalatine (sphenopalatine) fossa is the indented area medial to the pterygomaxillary fissure, leading into the sphenopalatine foramen. It communicates with the nasal and oral cavities, infratemporal fossa, orbit, pharynx and middle cranial fossa through eight foramina.

DirectionCommunicates withVia
LaterallyInfratemporal fossaPterygomaxillary fissure
MediallyNasal cavitySphenopalatine foramen
AnteriorlyOrbitInferior orbital fissure
InferoposteriorlyNasopharynxPalatovaginal canal
InferiorlyOral cavityGreater palatine canal and foramen
PosterosuperiorlyMiddle cranial fossaForamen rotundum and the pterygoid canal

Contents

  • The maxillary division of CN V (V2) and its branches — posterior superior alveolar, middle superior alveolar, anterior superior alveolar and infraorbital
  • The pterygopalatine ganglion
  • The maxillary artery and its branches
Pterygopalatine ganglion: it is the parasympathetic ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII), supplying glands in the oral and nasal mucosa and the lacrimal gland. Sensory fibres of V2 pass through the ganglion without synapsing — these supply the nose, palate, tonsils and gingiva. Named V2 branches through it include the posterior superior alveolar and the greater and lesser palatine nerves.
Two nerves, one ganglion: this is a recurring trigeminal theme — a parasympathetic ganglion belonging to one cranial nerve sits on the branches of another. The same happens at the otic ganglion (IX on V3) and the submandibular ganglion (VII on the lingual nerve).

Lecture 9 · Part 7Maxillary Artery Revisited

  • One of the two terminal branches of the external carotid
  • Terminates as the infraorbital artery as it enters the orbit via the inferior orbital fissure
  • Follows a tortuous course, passing lateral to lateral pterygoid in about ⅔ of individuals
PartPositionBranch pattern
1 — MandibularBefore reaching lateral pterygoid5 branches, each of which enters a bone
2 — PterygoidAlong lateral pterygoid (medial or lateral to it)5 branches to soft tissue — 4 to the masticatory muscles, the 5th is the buccal
3 — PterygopalatineEnters the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissureBranches accompanying those of the pterygopalatine ganglion and each branch of the maxillary nerve
Count discrepancy between lectures: this slide says the pterygopalatine part gives 5 branches, while the blood supply lecture lists 6 (posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, descending palatine, sphenopalatine, artery of the pterygoid canal, pharyngeal). The 6-branch list is the one to learn — the "5" here appears to follow a scheme that omits the small pharyngeal branch.
BranchSupplies
Inferior alveolarMandibular molars and premolars, plus gingiva
MentalChin and gingiva
IncisiveMandibular incisors
Middle meningealDura of the anterior and middle cranial fossae
BuccalBuccinator, buccal mucosa and skin
Anterior and middle superior alveolarMaxillary incisors and canines, and the maxillary sinus
Posterior superior alveolarMaxillary molars and premolars, adjacent gingiva, and the maxillary sinus
Descending palatineVia the greater palatine (roof of the hard palate, nasal cavity, maxillary gingiva) and the lesser palatine (soft palate)
SphenopalatineParanasal sinuses, nasal conchae and septum
Note the anastomoses: there are multiple connections between branches of the ophthalmic, sphenopalatine and descending palatine arteries — which is why nosebleeds from Little's area can involve vessels from more than one source.
